title: Transitions for examples, emphasis and conclusions
subject: LANGUAGE
subtopic: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions

slides.title: Words that link ideas
slides.text:
**Transition words** join one idea to the next.

They help the reader know what is coming.

slides.title: Give an example
slides.text:
**For example** shows one small piece of a big idea.

I like fruit. **For example**, I eat dates every day.

slides.title: Show the end
slides.text:
**In the end** and **Finally** tell the reader you are finishing.

We played all day. **In the end**, we were tired and happy.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Read the sentence **before** the blank.
2. Read the sentence **with** the blank.
3. Is it one small piece of the idea before? Use **for example**.
4. Does it finish the story? Use **in the end**.

sentences.t: For example, we pick up litter.

example.explain:
Picking up litter is **one way** the class helps.

So **For example** fits. It shows one small piece of the big idea.

together.passage: My little sister is very kind. ___, she shares her toys with her friends. She also helps Mom in the kitchen.
together.stem: Which words fit best in the blank?
together.hint: Is sharing toys the end of a story? Or is it one way to be kind?
together.good: Yes! Sharing toys is one example of being kind.

sentences: My little sister is very kind.
___, she shares her toys with her friends.
She also helps Mom in the kitchen.
evidence.stem: The answer was: For example. Tap 2 sentences: the big idea and the example right after it.
evidence.wrong: This sentence adds one more kind act, but it has no blank. Find the big idea and the sentence with the blank.

checks.passage: We had a busy day at the beach. We swam in the sea. We built a sand castle. ___, we went home very tired.
checks.stem: Which words fit best in the blank?
checks.why: Going home is the last thing that happened. In the end shows the finish.

checks.passage: Many animals live in the desert. ___, lizards hide under the rocks.
checks.stem: Which words fit best in the blank?
checks.why: Lizards are one example of desert animals.

checks.passage: Omar likes sports. ___, he plays football every week.
checks.stem: Which words fit best in the blank?
checks.why: Football is one example of a sport Omar likes. The other words are for endings.

again.title: Small piece or the end?
again.text:
Ask one question about the sentence with the blank.

1. Is it **one piece** of the big idea? Use **for example**.
2. Is it the **last thing**? Use **in the end**.
again.example:
I love my town. **For example**, it has a big park.

We cooked and ate. **In the end**, we washed the plates.

slides.title: Signal the ending
slides.text:
Some transitions tell the reader: **the summary is coming**.

**In conclusion**, **to sum up**, **overall**, **in short** and **all in all** all do this job.

slides.title: A summary, not a new idea
slides.text:
After an ending transition, the sentence must **sum up** what you already said.

It should **not** bring in a brand-new detail.

slides.title: Mix them up
slides.text:
Good writers do not use **in conclusion** every time.

Try **overall** or **in short** for a short paragraph. Save **in conclusion** for the end of a longer piece.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the sentence with the blank.
2. Check: does it **repeat the big idea** in new words?
3. Find the details above it that it **adds up**.

If the sentence sums up those details, an ending transition fits.

sentences.t: Our school started recycling last year.
Every class has a blue box for paper.
Students bring empty bottles to a big bin near the gate.
Overall, recycling has made our school cleaner and greener.

example.explain:
The last sentence does not add a new detail. It **sums up** the paper boxes and the bottle bin.

So **Overall** is a good ending transition.

together.passage: Our school started a reading club this year. Every Monday, members meet in the library to talk about a book. Older students read aloud to younger ones. Each month, the club chooses a new book together. ___, the club has helped many students enjoy reading more.
together.stem: Which transition best fits the blank?
together.hint: Does the last sentence give a new example, or does it sum up the whole paragraph?
together.good: Yes! The last sentence sums up the club's good work, so In short fits.

sentences: Our school started a reading club this year.
Every Monday, members meet in the library to talk about a book.
Older students read aloud to younger ones.
Each month, the club chooses a new book together.
___, the club has helped many students enjoy reading more.
evidence.stem: The answer was: In short. Tap 2 detail sentences that the last sentence sums up.
evidence.wrong: This sentence introduces the club or is the summary itself. Find the details that the summary adds up.

checks.passage: Water keeps our bodies working well. It helps us stay cool on hot days. It carries food to every part of the body. It also helps us think clearly. ___, drinking enough water every day is good for our health.
checks.stem: Which transition best fits the blank?
checks.why: The last sentence sums up all the ways water helps us, so it needs an ending transition.

checks.passage: Our city's winter festival brings many events each year. There are concerts, food stalls and shows for families. Visitors come from other cities to join in.
checks.stem: Which sentence is the best ending for this paragraph?
options: To sum up, some shows start at nine.
To sum up, the food stalls sell sweets.
To sum up, visitors come from far away.
To sum up, the season fills the city with fun for everyone.
checks.why: Only this sentence sums up the whole paragraph. The others add one small detail.

checks.passage: In conclusion, the trip was long. We drove for six hours. In conclusion, it was worth it because we saw the sea.
checks.stem: The writer used In conclusion twice. Which words could replace the second one?
checks.why: All in all also sums up, so it keeps the meaning and avoids repeating the same words.

again.title: The wrap-up test
again.text:
Read the last sentence by itself.

1. Could it be a **short answer** to "What was the whole paragraph about?"
2. If yes, put **in short**, **overall** or **to sum up** before it.
again.example:
Bees make honey. They help flowers grow. Many farms need them.

What was it all about? Bees are useful. **Overall, bees are very useful insects.**

slides.title: Transitions for examples
slides.text:
Use these to show a **specific case** of a general idea: **for example**, **for instance**, **such as**, **in particular**.

The idea comes first. The example comes after the transition.

slides.title: Transitions for emphasis
slides.text:
Use these to make a point **stronger**: **in fact**, **indeed**, **above all**, **most importantly**, **even**.

They tell the reader: this next part matters even more, or it is more surprising than you think.

slides.title: Which job is it?
slides.text:
1. Is the next sentence a **case** of the idea before it? Choose an **example** transition.
2. Does it **push the idea further** or correct a wrong belief? Choose an **emphasis** transition.
3. Read the sentence aloud with your choice. Does the meaning hold?

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
Your choice must match the link between **two sentences**.

1. Name the idea in the sentence before the blank.
2. Name what the sentence with the blank adds.
3. Ask: is it an example of that idea, or a stronger version of it?

Point to both sentences to prove your choice.

sentences.t: Many people think the desert is empty at night.
In fact, it is full of life after dark.
Foxes, owls and beetles come out when the air cools down.

example.explain:
The second sentence is not an example. It **corrects** a wrong belief and makes the point stronger.

So **In fact** is the right transition. The third sentence then gives examples.

together.passage: Many animals in Saudi Arabia have clever ways to survive the heat. ___, the Arabian oryx has a white coat that reflects sunlight. The sand cat rests in a burrow during the day and hunts at night. The spiny-tailed lizard digs deep tunnels where the ground stays cooler. These habits help them stay alive in one of the hottest places on Earth.
together.stem: Which transition best fits the blank?
together.hint: Is the oryx a result, a contrast, or one case of the general idea in the first sentence?
together.good: Yes! The oryx is one specific case of an animal with a clever way to survive the heat.

sentences: Many animals in Saudi Arabia have clever ways to survive the heat.
___, the Arabian oryx has a white coat that reflects sunlight.
The sand cat rests in a burrow during the day and hunts at night.
The spiny-tailed lizard digs deep tunnels where the ground stays cooler.
These habits help them stay alive in one of the hottest places on Earth.
evidence.stem: The answer was: For instance. Tap the general idea and the sentence that gives the first example of it.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is a later example or the ending. Find the general idea and the first example that follows it.

checks.passage: Some people believe that reading is only for school. ___, many adults read every day for fun and to learn new skills.
checks.stem: Which transition best fits the blank?
checks.why: The second sentence corrects a wrong belief and makes the point stronger, so In fact fits.

checks.passage: Healthy snacks give you energy for school. Fruits ___ bananas, apples and grapes are easy to carry in a lunch box.
checks.stem: Which words best fit the blank?
checks.why: Such as introduces examples of fruits inside the same sentence.

checks.passage: There are many ways to stay safe in the summer heat. Wear a hat and light clothes. Rest in the shade when you can. ___, drink water often, even before you feel thirsty.
checks.stem: Which transition best shows that the last tip is the most important?
checks.why: Above all tells the reader that this tip matters more than the others.

again.title: Example or stronger?
again.text:
Picture a staircase.

1. **Example** transitions stay on the **same step**: they show a case of the idea.
2. **Emphasis** transitions go **one step up**: they make the idea stronger or more surprising.
again.example:
Ahmed loves science. **For example**, he reads about planets. (same step)

Ahmed loves science. **In fact**, he wants to be an astronaut. (one step up)

slides.title: A toolbox of transitions
slides.text:
Strong writing uses **different kinds** of transitions, each for its own job:

**Example:** for instance, to illustrate
**Emphasis:** indeed, above all, in fact
**Contrast:** however, on the other hand
**Cause and effect:** as a result, consequently
**Conclusion:** ultimately, in conclusion, overall

slides.title: Choose by meaning
slides.text:
A transition is a **promise** about how two ideas are related. If the promise is wrong, the reader is confused.

"However" promises a contrast. If the next idea agrees with the last, "however" breaks that promise.

slides.title: Vary and place well
slides.text:
1. Avoid using the same transition again and again.
2. Put a transition where the **logic** changes, not in every sentence.
3. Check the whole passage: does each transition match the link between its two ideas?

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
For each blank, look at the idea **before** and the idea **after**.

1. Agree and add an example? **Example** transition.
2. Turn in a new direction? **Contrast** transition.
3. Show what happened because of it? **Cause and effect**.
4. Pull the whole passage together? **Conclusion**.

The sentences on both sides of the blank are your evidence.

sentences.t: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity.
Sunny countries, for instance, can produce large amounts of solar power.
However, panels make little power at night.
As a result, engineers are building better batteries to store energy for later.
Ultimately, sunlight could become a main source of power for many homes.

example.explain:
Each transition does a different job. **For instance** gives an example, **However** turns to a problem, **As a result** shows what the problem led to, and **Ultimately** concludes.

The passage uses several types, and each one matches the logic.

together.passage: Volunteering helps both the community and the volunteer. (1) ___, young people who clean beaches protect sea animals and keep the shore beautiful for everyone. (2) ___, volunteering can take time away from homework and rest. Even so, many students say they feel happier and more confident after helping others. (3) ___, giving a few hours each month can make a real difference to a town and to the person who gives.
together.stem: Which set of transitions best fits blanks (1), (2) and (3)?
options: (1) As a result (2) For example (3) However
(1) However (2) As a result (3) In fact
together.hint: Blank (1) begins a case of the first idea. Blank (2) turns to a downside. Blank (3) pulls everything together.
together.good: Yes! For instance gives an example, However marks the downside, and Overall concludes.

sentences: Volunteering helps both the community and the volunteer.
(1) ___, young people who clean beaches protect sea animals and keep the shore beautiful for everyone.
(2) ___, volunteering can take time away from homework and rest.
Even so, many students say they feel happier and more confident after helping others.
(3) ___, giving a few hours each month can make a real difference to a town and to the person who gives.
evidence.stem: Blank (2) needs a contrast word. Tap the sentence with blank (2) and the sentence just before it that it turns away from.
evidence.wrong: Look at blank (2) and the sentence before it: one shows a benefit, the next shows a cost. That turn is the contrast.

checks.passage: Our city planted thousands of trees last year. As a result, some streets are now several degrees cooler in summer. As a result, birds have returned to the parks. As a result, people walk more.
checks.stem: How could the writer best improve this passage?
options: Replace two of the repeated transitions with different ones that fit, such as In addition and Indeed
Change every As a result to However
Add For example before the first sentence
checks.why: The writer repeats the same transition. Varying them, with words that still fit the logic, makes the writing smoother.

checks.passage: Smartphones can help students learn. A student can look up a word in seconds. ___, phones can also distract students from their work.
checks.stem: Which transition best fits the blank?
checks.why: The last sentence turns to a problem with phones, so a contrast transition is needed.

checks.passage: The old market had been empty for years. Then the town turned it into a weekend fair for local farmers and crafts. ___, the market is busier than it has been in decades. ___, some shops have reopened on the streets nearby.
checks.stem: Which pair best fits the two blanks, in order?
options: In conclusion / On the other hand
checks.why: Today marks the change in time, and In fact adds a stronger, surprising point. The other pairs break the logic.

again.title: Before and after
again.text:
Cover the blank with your finger. Read only the idea before and the idea after.

1. Same direction, more detail? **For instance**.
2. Same direction, stronger? **In fact**.
3. Opposite direction? **However**.
4. Because of it? **As a result**.
5. Wrapping up? **Overall**.
again.example:
It rained all week. ___, the football match was cancelled.

Before: rain. After: match cancelled. The second happened **because of** the first, so **As a result** fits.
